text: The 1960s in Denmark were prosperous, and inside that prosperity stood a boys' home running to a timetable nobody outside was checking. Two brothers are sent there. Jesper W. Nielsen spends his 119 minutes less on any single act of cruelty than on repetition: the bell, the roster, the headmaster called Heck, whose authority never has to argue for itself because nobody arrives to hear the argument. What the brothers keep is an imagination held between them, the last thing in the building that is theirs. It was named the best Danish film of its year, and it takes its material from real cases rather than from an invented monster, which is the harder thing to sit with. Monsters are unusual. Institutions are funded and staffed.

A fish that does not belong in Lake Victoria eats nearly everything that does, and its fillets are boxed for export while weapons come the other way. Hubert Sauper builds the film out of that single exchange and refuses to leave it, keeping to the water and the shore towns the trade has made, until the arrangement stops looking like an accident and starts looking like a system with a great many hands on it. His method is patient and unliterary: he asks people what they do for a living, lets each answer be reasonable on its own terms, and lets the reasonable answers stack into something nobody would defend whole. Austria financed it, the lake is in East Africa, the market is somewhere else again, and that geography is most of the argument. By the second hour the ecology has become an accounting problem with names attached.

The footage presents itself as found rather than made: shot by the people in it, on video, with nobody behind the camera hoping it will come out well. Harmony Korine gives 77 minutes to a small group of elderly vandals loose at the margins of a frayed America, and the commitment is to that format, which means no scenes to speak of, no arc, nobody positioned to explain anyone else. It is filed as comedy and as horror, and those are not alternating modes here but one set of images read at two distances. Viewers average it 4.9 out of ten, a figure that describes the encounter more honestly than praise would. It is registered as a British production, a small joke on a film so thoroughly located in American margins, and it holds its subjects for exactly as long as the joke takes to stop working.

A one-man airship, an English inventor who designed it, and a jungle canopy he means to float just above rather than fly over. Werner Herzog stays with that ambition for 90 minutes, long enough to establish that the aircraft is the means and the wish is the subject: not exploration, not science with a grant number attached, but the desire to hang quietly a few metres over leaves nobody has stood on. The inventor is not collected as an eccentric. His design is treated as a proposition that deserves a test, and the test as something with consequences for the man strapped inside. The DOX:AWARD list carries the film, which suits a documentary whose entire drama is whether a thing one person drew will lift. The obsession here is quiet, well-mannered and completely unreasonable.

Christoffer has a wife, a life in Stockholm and no intention of going back. Then his father dies, the family firm is close to bankruptcy, and his mother makes the request that is not really a request. Per Fly gives 116 minutes to what happens to a man's days once he says yes: the meetings, the arithmetic of a company that cannot afford everyone in it, the way a marriage rearranges itself around a job that was supposed to be temporary. Duty is not a virtue in this film, and it is not a trap either. It is a job description, handed over at the worst available moment by the person best placed to know he will accept. What Per Fly is after is the hour a life turns into a position, with a desk, a payroll and a man who used to live somewhere else.

The old shepherd sweeps dust from the church floor and drinks it in his water, every day, as medicine. Michelangelo Frammartino sets the film in a Calabrian village high on a hill that most people left long ago, and builds it from the plain sequence of a working day: goats out, goats back, a body failing on a schedule of its own. Eighty-eight minutes, and the attention is distributed oddly and on purpose, so that the man, the animals and the hillside carry comparable weight and none of them is obviously the story. Italian cinema gave it the David di Donatello for direction, a strange prize for a film with so little visible directing in it, and the correct one. Belief is never examined here. It is what a man does at the end of a day, with a glass in his hand.

When the strike lands, everyone else moves away from it; these men drive toward it. The White Helmets of Aleppo were not soldiers or professionals, only residents who decided that pulling people out of rubble was a job somebody had to hold, and the film follows three of them, Khaled, Subhi and Mahmoud, through the parts of the work that are not emergencies: the waiting, the talk, the hours in which a city under attack is merely a city. Across 101 minutes the question it keeps returning to is domestic rather than political. Leave, or stay. A man can hold both answers at once, and the question is put to him again every morning with a fresh set of facts. It took the World Cinema documentary grand jury prize at Sundance, and it is notably unimpressed by its own courage.

Martin Luther King Jr.'s sentences travelled, and one of the places they landed was a Danish classroom in 1969, where a boy concluded they applied to him. The gap between those two facts is the film. Niels Arden Oplev keeps the scale small: one school, one headmaster whose authority has never had to explain itself, one child who will not let a matter drop. Across 105 minutes the boy's seriousness is taken seriously, which is rarer than it sounds, and the adults are not enlarged into monsters but left as people protecting an arrangement that suits them. A jury of children gave the film their award for best live-action feature, which is the right constituency to have asked. The rhetoric is borrowed from far away. The risk is entirely local.

Men still take oil tankers apart by hand on a beach in Pakistan, and Michael Glawogger went to film them doing it. Workingman's Death is built in five parts, each headed like a chapter: HEROES in the illegal Ukrainian mines, GHOST among the Indonesian sulphur carriers, LIONS in a Nigerian slaughterhouse, BROTHERS on the tanker, FUTURE in a Chinese steel plant. That sequence is all the commentary there is. Its premise is that heavy physical labour has not left the world, only the parts of the world that get photographed, and neither pity nor celebration is on offer across the 122 minutes. The work is given the time the work takes. The men doing it are allowed to be very good at it, which is the detail that stays.

In 1973 eleven people were put on a raft in the middle of the Atlantic so that a scientist could observe how violence and attraction begin. Five men, six women, three months, one deck. Marcus Lindeen brings the survivors back together decades afterwards and sets what they say now against the archive the expedition left behind, and that pairing is the instrument: the voyage was designed to produce a result, the passengers were designed to be the data, and only one of those parties has spent forty years thinking about it. The film runs 97 minutes and keeps out of the way of the talking. What it recovers is less the crossing than the tone of people describing, carefully and still a little puzzled, what it was like to spend a season as somebody's hypothesis.

Jake Williams lives by himself in a wood in Aberdeenshire, and for 88 minutes Ben Rivers watches him get through the day. Hauling, mending, waiting, and the odd projects a man invents when nobody is expecting results. Rivers took his cue from Knut Hamsun's Pan, which puts the film nearer to a mood than to a case study: the seasons turn without being announced, and Williams argues nothing about how a person ought to live. The interest is in duration. A documentary of this length could have covered a life, and this one covers a routine instead, on the grounds that a routine holds more weather, more mess and more invention than a biography would have found room for. What accumulates is a working knowledge of one man's afternoons.

Barbara has been married twice, both husbands were vicars, and both are in the ground. When Mr. Paul arrives on the Faroe Islands to take up his benefice, the warnings reach him along with the welcome. Denmark put the film forward to the Academy Awards that year; Nils Malmros takes 143 minutes over the courtship, which is about the right length for a place where nothing can be done privately. The church is the employer. Thorshavn is small. A widow's reputation is public property, maintained by people convinced of their own kindness. The film declines to settle the question the parish settled long ago about her, watching instead a man try to hold his office and his wanting in one pair of hands, with a rival named Andreas Heide arriving to test the grip.
